questions.stem: In E. coli, the lac operon is transcribed at high levels only when lactose is present and glucose is scarce. A mutant strain produces a repressor that cannot bind the operator. Predict transcription in this strain when lactose is absent and glucose is abundant.
options: High transcription, because lactose is the only signal the operon requires.
No transcription, because glucose is abundant so CAP cannot bind the promoter.
Low-level constitutive transcription, because repression is lost but CAP-cAMP activation is still missing.
High transcription, because the mutant repressor now recruits RNA polymerase to the promoter.
questions.why: Losing operator binding makes the operon unrepressible, but with glucose abundant cAMP is low, so CAP does not activate. The result is a low baseline rate, not full induction.

questions.stem: "The new cellphone policy has reduced hallway disruptions, and its supporters deserve credit for that. But a policy that trades quiet hallways for students who cannot sit with an unanswered question is not a compromise; it is a trade we cannot afford." The concession mainly serves to
options: establish the writer's authority as a district official
acknowledge a real benefit before arguing that its cost is disqualifying
weaken the writer's own position so the argument appears even-handed
shift responsibility for the policy onto its supporters
questions.why: Granting the genuine benefit makes the following claim harder to dismiss as partisan, so the rebuttal lands with more force. Conceding a point you then outweigh is a strength, not a retreat.

questions.stem: Cells are grown for one generation in a medium with heavy nitrogen, then moved to light medium and allowed to replicate twice more. After the second round in light medium, what fraction of the DNA molecules carries at least one heavy strand?
options: One-half, because each parental strand stays intact and appears in two of the four daughter molecules.
One-quarter, because the heavy label is diluted by half in each round of replication.
All four, because heavy nitrogen is redistributed among every newly built strand.
None, because replication is dispersive and fragments the original label.
questions.why: Replication is semiconservative: the two original heavy strands each pair with a new light strand, giving two hybrid molecules out of four. The label never disappears, it is just outnumbered.

questions.stem: "The proposal asks the board to fund a new gymnasium, to hire three counselors, and it also wants a later start time." Which revision fixes the faulty parallelism without changing the meaning?
options: The proposal asks the board to fund a new gymnasium, to hire three counselors, and asking for a later start time.
The proposal asks the board to fund a new gymnasium, hiring three counselors, and a later start time.
The proposal asks the board to fund a new gymnasium and to hire three counselors and also wants a later start time.
The proposal asks the board to fund a new gymnasium, to hire three counselors, and to adopt a later start time.
questions.why: The series must be three parallel infinitives: to fund, to hire, to adopt. Only that revision keeps all three items in the same grammatical form without splitting the sentence's logic.

questions.stem: A point mutation changes the codon UAC to UAA in the middle of an mRNA. Predict the most likely effect on the protein and the mechanism behind it.
options: A single amino acid substitution, because the ribosome reads UAA as tyrosine.
Premature termination of translation, because UAA is a stop codon read by a release factor.
A frameshift, because inserting a stop codon shifts the reading frame by one base.
No change, because the third base is degenerate and never affects the amino acid.
questions.why: UAA is one of the three stop codons, so the ribosome terminates early and releases a truncated peptide. Degeneracy protects against some third-base changes but cannot rescue a codon turned into a stop.

questions.stem: "The committee reviewed the budget for two hours. It approved every line — every single line — in eleven minutes." The punctuation in the second sentence mainly works to
options: list the specific budget items the committee approved
soften the criticism by emphasizing the committee's diligence
isolate the repeated phrase so the speed and unanimity land as the point
signal that the writer is quoting the committee's minutes verbatim
questions.why: The dashes set the repetition apart from the sentence's frame, forcing a pause that makes the eleven-minute approval the punchline. The punctuation is doing argumentative work, not decoration.

questions.stem: A cell line carries a mutation that removes the requirement to repair DNA damage before passing the G1/S checkpoint. Cells with damaged DNA continue into S phase. Which best predicts the long-term consequence for this population?
options: Accumulating mutations and chromosomal instability, because damaged templates are replicated repeatedly.
Arrest in metaphase, because the spindle checkpoint can no longer be satisfied.
Normal division, because S phase proofreads and corrects all damage as it copies.
Apoptosis in every daughter cell, because p53 is activated by the unrepaired damage.
questions.why: Replicating a damaged template converts lesions into permanent mutations and can generate breaks during mitosis. The checkpoint exists because S phase cannot repair what it copies past.

questions.stem: "We have waited through two budget cycles. We have waited through three superintendents. We have waited through every promise this board has made about transparency." The repetition mainly functions to
options: supply specific evidence that each promise was broken
establish the speaker's unfamiliarity with the board's record
build cumulative pressure so the final clause arrives as a culmination
create a comic tone that undercuts the speaker's seriousness
questions.why: Anaphora accumulates force across parallel clauses, making the third item feel like the sum of the first two. The pattern is the argument: patience has a limit.

questions.stem: A mother with blood type AB and a father with blood type O have a child. Which statement about the child's blood type is correct, and why?
options: The child must be type A, because A is dominant to B.
The child can be type AB, because both parental alleles are codominant.
The child must be type O, because O is recessive to both A and B.
The child is type A or type B, because the type O parent can contribute only an O allele.
questions.why: The AB parent gives either A or B, and the O parent can only give O, so the child is AO or BO and expresses A or B. Type AB is impossible without a B allele from the second parent.

questions.stem: "The board's listening tour has all the substance of a Potemkin village: well-lit facades, no residents behind them." The allusion mainly works by
options: inviting comparison to a convincing surface that conceals an absence
attributing the board's motives to a foreign government
supplying statistical proof that the tour was staged
praising the board's skill at public relations
questions.why: The allusion imports a whole story of constructed appearances, letting one phrase carry the charge of fakery. It is a comparison, not evidence.

questions.stem: An affected man has an unaffected daughter. She has two affected sons and one unaffected son. No female in the family is affected, and the affected men's wives have no family history. Which pattern best explains this?
options: Autosomal dominant, because the trait appears in every generation.
X-linked recessive, because affected men pass the allele through carrier daughters to grandsons.
Autosomal recessive, because the trait skips a generation.
Mitochondrial, because only males express the trait.
questions.why: Sons get their X only from the mother, so a carrier daughter produces affected sons while remaining unaffected herself. Autosomal recessive would require unrelated wives to be carriers, which the pedigree rules out.

questions.stem: "The district did not cut the program; it right-sized it, reallocating resources toward higher-need priorities." A reader who objects to the cut would most likely argue that this phrasing
options: includes too much budget detail to follow
concedes that the program was ineffective
is too informal for an official statement
replaces a concrete loss with language that obscures who was harmed
questions.why: Right-sizing names an action without naming its victims, which is the work a euphemism does. The objection is to abstraction that removes accountability, not to tone.

questions.stem: A storm reduces a beetle population from 10,000 to 40. Survival was unrelated to shell color. Twenty years later the population numbers 5,000 and differs sharply in allele frequency from the original. Which best explains the change?
options: Natural selection, because only the best-adapted forty beetles survived the storm.
Gene flow, because beetles migrated in from neighboring islands afterward.
Genetic drift, because a small surviving sample shifted frequencies by chance.
Mutation, because new alleles arose rapidly during the population's recovery.
questions.why: When survival is random with respect to the trait, a severe bottleneck changes frequencies by sampling error, not fitness. Selection is ruled out by the stem itself.

questions.stem: "Dr. Alvarez, who has studied adolescent sleep for twenty years, argues that later start times improve attendance. The board should adopt her recommendation." The argument would be strengthened most by
options: adding that Dr. Alvarez speaks often at national conferences
showing that her claim rests on data from districts comparable to this one
noting that most parents in the district already agree with her
quoting her credentials at greater length
questions.why: The gap is transferability: expertise in general does not establish that the finding applies here. Comparable-district data closes that gap; more prestige and more agreement do not.

questions.stem: On a cold morning a student's core temperature stays near 37 C while skin temperature falls sharply. Which combination best explains the response?
options: Peripheral vasoconstriction and shivering, triggered by hypothalamic detection of cooled blood.
Peripheral vasodilation and sweating, triggered by cooled blood reaching the hypothalamus.
Reduced metabolic rate and vasodilation, which conserve heat by lowering blood flow.
Increased sweating and piloerection, which generate heat through evaporation.
questions.why: Constricting skin vessels keeps warm blood in the core and shivering generates metabolic heat, both under negative feedback from the hypothalamus. Vasodilation and sweating are heat-loss responses, the opposite of what cold requires.

questions.stem: "My opponent wants to add ten minutes to the school day. Apparently she believes students should have no time for sports, music, or rest — just more worksheets." The reasoning is flawed mainly because it
options: relies on statistics that cannot be verified
generalizes from a single student's experience
assumes that longer school days never improve learning
misstates the opponent's position as an extreme she did not propose
questions.why: Ten extra minutes is not the elimination of sports and rest; the argument refutes a position nobody holds. That substitution is what makes it a straw man rather than a disagreement.

questions.stem: Three DNA samples are run on the same gel. Sample 2's band travels farther than sample 1's, and sample 3 produces two distinct bands. Which interpretation is best supported?
options: Sample 2 contains more DNA than sample 1, which is why it migrates farther.
Sample 2's fragments are shorter than sample 1's, and sample 3 holds fragments of two different lengths.
Sample 3 is contaminated, because a clean sample yields only one band.
Sample 2 carries a stronger negative charge than sample 1 and so moves faster.
questions.why: Migration distance depends on fragment size, with shorter fragments running farther through the gel matrix. DNA has a uniform charge-to-mass ratio, so charge differences do not explain separation.

questions.stem: "Either we eliminate the late-bus route entirely or we accept that the district will never balance its budget." The argument's central flaw is that it
options: presents two options as exhaustive when other savings are possible
attacks the character of the transportation director
generalizes from one year of budget data
assumes the budget has already been independently audited
questions.why: The sentence offers a binary where a range of alternatives exists, so rejecting one option is made to force the other. Naming only two choices is the whole of the error.

questions.stem: A desert mammal produces urine far more concentrated than its blood plasma. Which structure and mechanism best explain this capability?
options: A short loop of Henle that dilutes the medulla so water can follow solutes out.
Glomerular filtration that removes water before solutes are reabsorbed.
A long loop of Henle that builds a steep medullary gradient, plus ADH-driven water reabsorption.
Active secretion of water into the collecting duct against its concentration gradient.
questions.why: A long loop of Henle creates the deep osmotic gradient in the medulla, and ADH makes the collecting duct permeable so water leaves. Water is never actively secreted; it moves osmotically.

questions.stem: "The schedule must be working, because it is clearly effective and producing the results we wanted." The reasoning is circular because it
options: cites research that contradicts its own conclusion
restates the conclusion in place of evidence
shifts from a claim about schedules to a claim about students
relies on an unrepresentative sample of schools
questions.why: Effective and producing results are the conclusion in other words, so nothing independent supports the claim. Evidence would have to come from outside the assertion itself.

questions.stem: Months after vaccination, a student is exposed to the pathogen. Antibody levels rise within two days, far faster than after the first exposure. Which best explains the rapid rise?
options: The vaccine remained in the blood and neutralized the pathogen directly.
Innate immunity now recognizes the pathogen without any prior exposure.
Memory B cells were converted to plasma cells before the exposure occurred.
Memory B cells specific to the pathogen proliferated and differentiated into antibody-secreting plasma cells.
questions.why: The secondary response is fast because a large clone of specific memory cells already exists and needs only activation, not selection from scratch. Memory cells do not sit pre-differentiated as plasma cells.

questions.stem: "Nearly everyone in the senior class signed the petition, so the petition must be right about the schedule." The argument fails because
options: the signatures have not been independently verified
the senior class is too small a group to survey
how many people hold a view is not evidence that the view is true
petitions are an ineffective form of civic participation
questions.why: Agreement measures popularity, not accuracy, so the premise cannot establish the claim. Verification of signatures would not fix the inferential gap either.

questions.stem: A plant is moved to a humid chamber with still air. Transpiration falls sharply within an hour. Which best explains the drop and its effect on the xylem water column?
options: The leaf-to-air vapor gradient shrinks, so less tension pulls the xylem column upward.
Stomata close, so root pressure alone now pushes water to the leaves faster.
The xylem sap thickens in humid air, blocking flow until the plant dries.
Higher humidity increases adhesion, which pulls water upward more quickly.
questions.why: Transpiration is driven by the vapor pressure difference between leaf interior and air; humid, still air flattens that gradient and reduces the pulling tension. Root pressure is far too weak to replace it.

questions.stem: A writer addressing a school board opens: "You have thirty minutes and a long agenda, so I will make three claims and give each one a number." This opening mainly
options: signals that the argument will be long and heavily detailed
adapts the structure to the audience's constraints to earn a hearing
concedes that the writer's evidence is weak
shifts responsibility for the decision onto the board
questions.why: Naming the audience's limit and organizing around it is a credibility move: it promises the listener a manageable cost. It says nothing about the strength of the evidence.

questions.stem: A neuron is depolarized to threshold. Voltage-gated Na+ channels open, Na+ enters, and the membrane potential climbs toward +30 mV. Which best explains why the rise stops there?
options: K+ channels close, which prevents any further depolarization.
The Na+/K+ pump reverses direction and removes Na+ from the axon.
Na+ channels stay open but the membrane returns to rest by simple diffusion.
Na+ channels inactivate and voltage-gated K+ channels open, so K+ efflux repolarizes the membrane.
questions.why: The peak reflects Na+ channel inactivation plus delayed opening of K+ channels, and the resulting K+ efflux repolarizes the cell. The pump restores gradients afterward; it does not cause the falling phase.

questions.stem: "Through three hearings, two rejected drafts, and a petition signed by four hundred parents, the board arrived at its decision." Compared with a sentence that states the decision first, this structure mainly
options: delays the main clause so the effort behind the decision becomes the reader's focus
shortens the sentence so the decision seems abrupt
conceals the subject in order to avoid assigning responsibility
converts a narrative into a causal argument
questions.why: Holding the main clause until the end makes the reader travel the process before reaching the outcome. That delay is the emphasis, not a concealment of the actor.

questions.stem: Yeast introduced into a sealed flask grow slowly, then rapidly, then level off at about two million cells. Which best explains the leveling off?
options: The yeast exhausted its mutation rate and stopped dividing.
The population reached exponential growth, which is stable by definition.
Resources became limiting, so births no longer exceeded deaths.
Predators in the flask began consuming the yeast.
questions.why: Logistic growth plateaus when nutrient or space limits make per-capita growth fall to zero. Exponential growth has no plateau, so it cannot explain a stable ceiling.

questions.stem: "Later start times tend to improve attendance in most districts that have adopted them, though the effect varies with bus schedules." Compared with "Later start times improve attendance," this sentence mainly
options: removes the writer's claim entirely
makes the claim impossible to falsify
weakens the claim by admitting there is no evidence
limits the claim's scope so it survives known counterexamples
questions.why: Qualifiers bound the claim to a tendency and a population, which is what makes it defensible against exceptions. Precision here is strength, not retreat.

questions.stem: Phosphorylation of glucose by hexokinase is endergonic on its own. Which best explains how the reaction proceeds in a cell?
options: The reaction releases enough heat during binding to drive itself forward.
ATP hydrolysis is coupled to the reaction, supplying free energy that makes the overall process exergonic.
The enzyme lowers the reaction's free-energy change until it reaches zero.
The reaction is driven by a decrease in entropy in the cytoplasm.
questions.why: Coupling to ATP hydrolysis makes the combined reaction exergonic, driving glucose phosphorylation. Enzymes lower activation energy but never change the sign of delta-G.

questions.stem: A student writes: "In 'The Checkpoint,' Okonkwo argues that standardized testing narrows curricula by rewarding recall, illustrating the claim with a district that cut lab science." This sentence mainly
options: summarizes the author's claim along with the evidence used to support it
evaluates whether Okonkwo's evidence is sufficient
compares Okonkwo to a second author on the same topic
states the student's own position about testing
questions.why: A precis reports what the writer argues and how it is supported, without judging the argument. Evaluation and the student's own view are separate moves.

questions.stem: Sea otters are removed from a kelp forest. Urchin populations explode, kelp cover collapses, and fish that shelter in the kelp decline. Which term best describes the otter's role?
options: Primary producer, because otters convert energy for the rest of the food web.
Invasive species, because removing them destabilized the community.
Apex predator whose removal has no measurable community-level effect.
Keystone species, because its removal restructured the entire community.
questions.why: A keystone species has influence out of proportion to its abundance, and losing it cascades through the community. Otters are consumers, not producers, and they were native, so not invasive.

questions.stem: "The data are unambiguous. Enrollment fell 18 percent. The board, however, described the decline as a 'transitional recalibration.'" The shift in registers mainly
options: shows that the writer endorses the board's phrasing
proves the enrollment figures were miscalculated
sets plain fact against euphemism so the spin is exposed
indicates the writer is unsure which figure is correct
questions.why: Flat declaratives measured against bureaucratic abstraction make the board's wording look like evasion without the writer having to say so. The register contrast is the argument.

questions.stem: A spherical cell doubles its diameter while keeping its shape. Which best predicts the effect on its ability to exchange materials across the plasma membrane?
options: Exchange improves, because membrane area doubles along with volume.
Exchange declines, because volume grows about eightfold while membrane area grows only about fourfold.
Exchange is unchanged, because area and volume increase in the same proportion.
Exchange improves, because a larger cell contains more organelles to process materials.
questions.why: Area scales with the square of the radius and volume with the cube, so doubling the diameter cuts surface area per unit volume in half. That is why exchange efficiency falls as cells get larger.
